Transferring the disability tax credit to a supporting relative in 2026: how much moves, and the caregiver amount

A worked guide to moving the unused 2026 disability amount from a dependant to the parent, child or other relative who supports them: who qualifies, the CRA worksheet that decides how much is left to transfer, the child supplement, the Canada caregiver amount, splitting between supporters, when the supporter has too little tax to use it, and CRA statistics on who claims. Six charts and an editable model.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 26 October 2026 · 10 min read
Sources reviewed 26 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Original illustration of the 2026 federal disability amount (line 31600) transferred to a supporting person (line 31800), using the 2025 Federal Worksheet chart with 2026 amounts. The transferable part is the lesser of the dependant’s disability amount and that amount plus their line 98 credits minus their taxable income. Line 98 here includes only the basic personal amount, the Canada employment amount and base CPP and EI credits on the employment income entered; age, pension, caregiver, home buyers’ and other amounts the dependant may have are left out, so the transfer may be understated for a dependant with them. For a child under 18 the CAD 6,032 supplement is reduced by child care and attendant care expenses above CAD 3,533. The Canada caregiver amount for an infirm dependant 18 or older is CAD 8,773, reduced by the dependant’s net income above CAD 20,601. Credits are 14% of the amounts and only reduce federal tax the supporter actually owes after their own basic, CPP, EI and employment credits. Provincial and territorial credits, the spouse transfer on Schedule 2 (line 32600), the eligible dependant amount, medical expenses and the attendant-care rules in Guide RC4065 are left out.

The central idea

For 2026 the disability amount is CAD 10,341 (up to CAD 16,373 for a child under 18). A supporting relative can claim only the part the dependant does not need: the lesser of the disability amount and that amount plus the dependant’s basic credits minus their taxable income. An adult dependant with little income may also make the supporter eligible for a Canada caregiver amount of up to CAD 8,773. Both are worth 14% federally, and only against tax the supporter actually owes.

01

What the transfer is

The disability tax credit (DTC) is a non-refundable credit for a person with a severe and prolonged impairment whose Form T2201 has been approved by the CRA. It is claimed on line 31600 of that person’s return. Many people who qualify have little or no taxable income, so the credit would be wasted on their own return. The tax system lets the unused part move to someone who supports them:

  • Line 31800, for a dependant who is your (or your spouse’s) parent, grandparent, child, grandchild, brother, sister, aunt, uncle, niece or nephew, or for whom you claimed or could have claimed the eligible dependant amount.
  • Line 32600 (Schedule 2), when the person with the disability is your spouse or common-law partner. That route is separate and is not modelled here.

The 2026 figures are CRA’s published amounts after 2.0% indexation. The 2026 child maximum (CAD 10,341 + 6,032) and the caregiver end point (CAD 8,773 + 20,601) are derived; the same sums for 2025 match the CAD 16,052 and CAD 28,798 printed on the 2025 forms. At 14%, the base amount is worth CAD 1,447.74 of federal tax and the child maximum CAD 2,292.22.

02

Who can claim it

Under the CRA rules for line 31800 you can claim all or part of a dependant’s disability amount if all of these apply:

  • The CRA has approved Form T2201 for the dependant for the year.
  • The dependant was resident in Canada at any time in the year.
  • They depended on you for all or some of the basic necessities of life, such as food, shelter and clothing, on a regular and consistent basis.
  • They do not need all of the amount to reduce their own tax.
  • You claimed, or could have claimed, the eligible dependant amount (line 30400) for them, or the Canada caregiver amount for an infirm dependant 18 or older (line 30450), in the CRA’s “could have if they had no income” sense.

For a child under 18, the parent or guardian approved on the T2201 makes the claim. You cannot claim it if the person’s spouse or common-law partner already claims the disability amount or any other non-refundable credit (other than medical expenses) for them, and generally not if you pay support for that child. Several supporters may split the claim, but together they cannot claim more than the dependant’s maximum, and nobody can split it with a person who claimed the eligible dependant amount for that dependant.

A separate rule matters for families paying for care: if full-time care in a nursing home, or attendant care beyond the limited amount, is claimed as a medical expense for the person, nobody can claim the disability amount for them that year. The CRA’s Medical Expenses guide allows attendant-care wages of up to CAD 10,000 (CAD 20,000 in the year of death) alongside the disability amount; families with large care bills should compare both routes.

03

How much is left to transfer

The CRA’s Federal Worksheet for line 31800 works it out in three steps:

  1. Start with the dependant’s disability amount (CAD 10,341, or more for a child under 18).
  2. Add the dependant’s line 98 amount: the total of their own basic personal amount, age amount, spouse and dependant amounts, CPP and EI credits, Canada employment amount, pension income amount and the other credits listed before line 31600 on the return.
  3. Subtract the dependant’s taxable income. The transfer is the lesser of the disability amount and the result (not below zero).

In plain terms: the dependant keeps just enough of the disability amount, together with their other credits, to bring their federal tax to zero, and the rest can move. As long as the dependant’s taxable income is below their own line 98 credits, the whole disability amount transfers.

The model’s default is an adult child, 24, with CAD 24,000 of net income, CAD 18,000 of it from a part-time job, supported by a parent with CAD 85,000 of employment income.

The dependant’s own federal tax before the disability amount is CAD 3,360 − 14% × CAD 18,964.15 = CAD 705.02, which is exactly 14% of the CAD 5,035.85 they keep, so the worksheet leaves them owing nothing federally. The parent has about CAD 10,458 of federal tax left after their own basic credits, enough to use the CAD 1,495.08 in full. In the model, line 98 includes only the basic personal amount and the credits from employment income; a dependant with other amounts would keep less and transfer more.

04

What happens as the dependant earns more

The first chart moves the dependant’s income with everything else fixed. Three ranges matter:

  • Below the dependant’s own line 98 credits (about CAD 18,964 in the default), the whole CAD 10,341 transfers.
  • Above that, each extra dollar of taxable income reduces the transfer by a dollar, because the dependant now needs that much more of the credit. With CAD 18,000 of employment income the transfer reaches zero at about CAD 29,305.
  • The caregiver amount runs on a separate clock: the full CAD 8,773 until the dependant’s net income passes CAD 20,601, then down a dollar per dollar to zero at CAD 29,374.

For a dependant with no income at all, the parent can claim CAD 10,341 + CAD 8,773 = CAD 19,114, worth CAD 2,675.96 federally. At CAD 24,000 the dependant uses part of the disability credit themselves, so the family total is CAD 705.02 + CAD 1,495.08 = CAD 2,200.10: less in the parent’s hands, but the dependant also pays no federal tax on CAD 24,000.

05

A child under 18: the supplement and care expenses

For a child under 18 at the end of the year, the disability amount includes a supplement of up to CAD 6,032, reduced by child care and attendant care expenses claimed for the child (by anyone, for example as child care expenses or medical expenses) above CAD 3,533. The total therefore runs from CAD 16,373 down to the CAD 10,341 base once those expenses reach CAD 9,565.

  • No care expenses claimed: CAD 16,373, worth CAD 2,292.22 at 14%.
  • CAD 5,000 of care expenses: CAD 6,032 − (CAD 5,000 − 3,533) = CAD 4,565 supplement; total CAD 14,906, worth CAD 2,086.84.

A child with no income needs none of it, so the whole amount transfers to the parent approved on the T2201. The caregiver amount on line 30450 is for dependants 18 or older; for an infirm child under 18, a separate CAD 2,740 amount (line 30500) applies and is not modelled here.

06

When the supporter cannot use it

The transfer moves an amount, not cash. It becomes valuable only if the supporter has federal tax to reduce. In the default, a parent with CAD 20,000 of employment income has only CAD 126.59 of federal tax left after the basic personal amount, Canada employment amount and CPP and EI credits. The CAD 1,495.08 credit would be cut to CAD 126.59 and the other CAD 1,368.49 would be lost: it does not go back to the dependant, and it does not carry forward.

That is why, when two relatives support the same person, it is usually better for the one with more tax to claim, or to split so that each claim fits within each claimant’s tax. A 50/50 split in the default gives each claimant CAD 5,339.58 of amounts and CAD 747.54 of credit, the same CAD 1,495.08 in total, provided each has that much tax. The model’s share input shows the effect for one claimant.

The line 31800 average is above the 2024 base amount (CAD 9,872) because transfers for children include the supplement and one return can include more than one dependant. Measured against all returns in each total-income range, line 31800 claims rise from about 6 per 1,000 returns under CAD 10,000 to about 24 per 1,000 at CAD 150,000–249,999. That pattern fits transfers going to the relative who has tax to reduce, but the table counts returns, not families, and does not show why people claim or not. Counts are rounded to the nearest ten.

08

A practical checklist

  • Get the T2201 approved first. Nothing transfers until the CRA approves it; approval can cover past years.
  • File the dependant’s return, even with little income, so their taxable income and line 98 credits are on record; the transfer is calculated from them.
  • Check the caregiver amount for an adult dependant whose net income is below CAD 29,374.
  • Choose the claimant with enough federal tax, or split between supporters so each claim can be used.
  • Watch large care bills. Claiming full-time nursing-home or unlimited attendant care as a medical expense rules out the disability amount for that year; compare both routes.
  • Remember the province. Provincial credits have their own amounts and rates and transfer through the provincial forms.

09

Limits of the model

The model is federal only and uses 2026 amounts with the structure of the 2025 worksheet. It treats net income as taxable income for both people and includes in the dependant’s line 98 only the basic personal amount, Canada employment amount and base CPP and EI credits on the employment income entered; age, pension, home buyers’ and other amounts are left out. The supporter’s tax is estimated from 2026 brackets after the same basic credits, so other credits that would use up the supporter’s tax first are ignored. It does not model the spouse transfer (Schedule 2), the eligible dependant amount, the line 30500 child amount, medical expenses, the attendant-care choice, provincial credits or the Registered Disability Savings Plan and Canada Disability Benefit, which use DTC eligibility but are separate programs. Use tax software or the CRA worksheets for an actual return.
